reason: E1 directly supports the formation of M–N bonds and a Pt-rich shell via ammonia annealing in a similar HEA system, and links these to enhanced durability. However, E1 is an electrocatalyst study under HDV conditions, not automotive exhaust with H2O/NO/thermal aging, so the extrapolation to those specific deactivation mechanisms is unsupported. E2 does not involve nitrogen doping or the claimed structural features and is irrelevant to the key premises.
premises: Thermal annealing in ammonia can introduce nitrogen into a multi-element alloy, forming M–N bonds.
Nitrogen doping can induce a Pt-rich shell on a multi-element alloy catalyst.
M–N bonds and a Pt-rich shell enhance electrochemical stability and durability.
These structural features can mitigate deactivation from water, NO, and thermal aging in exhaust conditions.
The approach is effective with low platinum-group-metal content.
